passage: At the community centre's Thursday phone class, Jasleen Bua held up her screen before Alka could begin. "Fifty people died of a new fever in Ludhiana this week! Everyone in my group sent it. I've forwarded it to my sisters." The others leaned in, worried. Alka sat beside her aunt. "Let's find where it started." Together they searched the headline and followed it back: a news report from another country, three years old, about a different illness. "Bua, fevers do come every monsoon," Alka said gently. "But fifty in one week here? The hospital, the paper, the councillor would all be talking about it, not just forwards." Jasleen Bua looked at her screen. "Then I'll send my sisters this old article." "And let the fever message stop with us?" Jasleen Bua nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where did the fever story actually come from?
qa.a: A news report from another country, three years old, about a different illness.

qa.q: What was Jasleen Bua feeling when holding up the screen?
qa.a: Jasleen Bua was alarmed and eager to warn family; everyone in the group had sent it, so it felt urgent and true.

qa.q: Why did Alka's choice to trace the source together work better than just calling it fake?
qa.a: Tracing it together let Jasleen Bua see the old report with her own eyes and decide, without feeling scolded in front of the class.

qa.q: How might the other learners in the class be affected by watching this?
qa.a: They were worried too, so seeing the claim traced back calmly may ease their fear and give them a way to check the next scary forward.

Dear Sahil Mama,
I saw how worried you were on the family call, and I don't want to brush that aside. You've sent the message about a gang taking children from Coimbatore schools to three groups, so I checked before doing the same.
The photo of the 'gang' is a still from an old film shoot; I found the original online. The voice note has no names, no school, no date. And I asked a friend who has taught in Coimbatore for twelve years. She has never known a child taken from a school gate there.
So I'm not forwarding it, and I'd gently ask you to pause too. Keep walking Chinnu to school, of course; he loves it.
Love,
Keerthana

passage: So, Pranav, you want the salt story. Fine. Last year my Nani's building group decided ordinary iodised salt was, quote, 'slowly poisoning the family.' Somebody's cousin posted it, eighty people shared it, and Nani phoned me at seven a.m. sounding shaky. Me, Ishita, the family 'computer person.' So I did what I always do. First, where did it start? I scrolled back through the forwards to the original: an unsigned image, no doctor's name, and a website that no longer existed. Second, how common is this, really? I asked Nani: in eighty years, had she known one person hurt by ordinary salt? She thought hard. 'No.' Her own doctor said the same at her next checkup. I didn't forward anything. I sat with Nani over tea and showed her the dead website. She said, 'Then why did everyone send it?' Good question, Nani.

qa.q: What time did Nani phone Ishita?
qa.a: At seven a.m.

qa.a: Nani was frightened, sounding shaky, because so many people in the building group had shared the warning.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's choices made the biggest difference for Nani, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with Nani over tea and showing the dead website let Nani see the weak source for herself, instead of just being told the message was wrong.

qa.q: What does Nani's question "Then why did everyone send it?" suggest about how she now sees the forwards?
qa.a: Nani is starting to see that many shares don't make something true, and is puzzled about why so many people passed it on. 🤍

passage: I'm Tejas, and on Sunday I watched my sister Meher deal with Dadi's water message. It said two hundred people in our city were in hospital from poisoned tap water and nobody should drink it. Dadi had it from three groups and wanted to send it to all her sisters. Meher didn't argue. She sat with the phone and searched the words from the message. Twenty minutes later she found the original: a newspaper report from a different city, three years old. Then she asked Dadi, "In seventy years, how often have you heard of tap water poisoning a whole city here?" Dadi thought. "Never." Meher didn't forward it anywhere. She made Dadi tea and showed her the old article slowly, on the big screen. I can't say what Dadi thought, but she put the phone down.

qa.q: How old was the original report that Meher found?
qa.a: It was three years old, from a different city.

qa.q: What does Dadi putting the phone down suggest she might be feeling?
qa.a: She may have felt reassured, or a little embarrassed, after seeing the old article and realising how rare such an event is.

qa.q: Which part of Meher's approach helped most with Dadi, and why?
qa.a: Asking how often Dadi had heard of this in seventy years let Dadi reach the answer herself, so she didn't feel scolded.

qa.q: How are Dadi's sisters affected by Meher choosing not to forward the message?
qa.a: They are spared a frightening evening of worrying about their drinking water, because the chain stopped with Dadi.

grounding: An adult traces a scare claim to its source, asks how common it is, stops the chain and explains gently to a relative.

Monday. Leela Masi sent a voice note to the family group at midnight: a gang was stealing kidneys from patients at the city hospital, and everyone should stay away. By morning, Chetan's mother had forwarded it twice.
Wednesday. Chetan, twenty-four, spent his lunch break tracing it. The voice gave no name, no ward, no date. He found the same words in a post from another country, years old. He asked a friend who worked at the hospital how often anything like it had ever been reported there. "Never," she said.
Saturday. At Masi's house, he didn't post a correction in the group. He sat beside her and said, "I know you sent it because you care about us." Then he showed her what he had found. Masi was quiet for a moment, then asked him to help her delete it.

qa.q: Where did Chetan find the same words as the voice note?
qa.a: He found them in a post from another country, years old.

qa.q: Why did Chetan begin by telling Masi he knew she sent it because she cares?
qa.a: He wanted her to feel understood rather than foolish, so she would be open to what he found.

qa.q: What was the turning point in stopping the chain, and why did it work?
qa.a: Chetan chose to talk to Masi in person instead of correcting her in the group, which let her change her mind without losing face.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had posted a blunt correction in the family group?
qa.a: Leela Masi might have felt embarrassed in front of everyone and defended the message instead of deleting it.

grounding: An adult traces a scare message to its origin, checks how often it happens, and gently stops a relative's forwarding.
